title: Painting behind a radiator with a radiator roller
subtitle: Paint the wall section behind a radiator without disconnecting the plumbing, using a long-handled slim roller and angled brush
excerpt: How to paint the wall behind a radiator without removing it. Covers cooling the radiator, cutting in at the edges with an angled brush, rolling the main area with a radiator roller, and allowing proper drying time.
sourceNotes: UK trade decorating practice. Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A slim foam or mohair roller mounted on a long-angled handle that allows it to reach into the narrow gap between a wall-mounted radiator and the wall behind. The slim width of the roller sleeve passes through the gap that a standard 9-inch roller cannot access. Often sold as part of a painting kit with an angled brush for the edges.

content.text: The wall behind a radiator stays unpainted or dirty unless the radiator is removed or a long-handled radiator roller is used. A radiator roller reaches through the gap between the radiator and wall without touching the plumbing. BEGINNER: patience and a slow pace; the tools do the work.

Turn the radiator off and allow it to cool completely before painting. Paint applied over a warm radiator dries too fast, leaving brush marks and an uneven finish. Lay a dust sheet on the floor beneath the radiator to catch any drips. Dust and wipe the wall behind the radiator with a slightly damp cloth to remove accumulated fluff and dirt, reaching in from the top and sides.

Use a small angled brush to cut in the paint at the top, bottom, and side edges behind the radiator. Feed the brush handle behind the radiator and work in short strokes along each edge. The 25 mm brush is slim enough to reach along the back of most panel radiators. Take care not to load the brush too heavily so that drips do not land on the front face of the radiator.

with paint from the tray. Feed the roller between the radiator and wall from the top, keeping the handle close to the radiator body. Roll up and down in vertical strokes covering the full height of the gap. Work across the full width in overlapping passes. Keep the paint load on the roller light to avoid drips.

Allow the first coat to dry fully before applying a second. One coat of emulsion rarely covers a colour change adequately, especially in a difficult-to-see area. Two thin coats give better coverage than one heavy coat and reduce the risk of drips landing on the radiator.

attrs.symptom: Paint drips run down the front face of the radiator
attrs.cause: The roller or brush was overloaded with paint.
attrs.fix: Wipe drips immediately with a damp cloth while the paint is wet. Keep the roller and brush lightly loaded and dab off excess on the tray edge before applying.

attrs.symptom: Roller cannot reach the bottom strip of wall above the skirting
attrs.cause: The radiator sits too close to the skirting board for the roller to pass through at the bottom.
attrs.fix: Use the angled brush for the bottom strip, feeding it between the radiator and skirting as far as possible. The bottom edge is rarely visible, so small coverage gaps are not critical.
